newsitem.title: BELGIUM: MEPs to attack Commission on environment plans.
newsitem.headline: MEPs to attack Commission on environment plans.

text.p: The European Commission can expect to be hauled over the coals on November 13 by Euro-MPs disappointed with what they say are ineffectual and unambitious proposals for environmental protection.

A report from the European Parliament's environment committee, due to be adopted by the Parliament next week, pours scorn on the Commission's proposals for reviewing and updating the 5th European Union environmental action programme (1992- 2000)-- COM(95)647.
"We are very disappointed," the report's author, Lone Dybkjaer, told Reuters.
She said the Commission's proposals were a backward step.

Two reports on the state of Europe's environment had been drawn up so to inform the discussion about updating the 5th action programme but the Commission had ignored their recommendations, Dybkjaer's report says.

Both the Commission's own report on what the 5th programme has achieved so far -- COM(95)624 -- and the European Environment Agency's report on "The State of the Environment in Europe" warn, as the Commission did in 1992, that the current approach is failing dismally to prevent the environment from deteriorating.

"The reports said the 5th action programme would not achieve its aims by the year 2000," Dybkjaer said, adding that the Commission was obliged by the programme to come up with new proposals for achieving these goals.

"It hasn't done that. It has made suggestions about general guidelines. But you cannot be sure you will reach your goals by making new guidelines. You have to have new, concrete plans and new time limits for action," the Danish Liberal insisted.
Dybkjaer's report calls for a string of amendments designed to improve the Commission proposal.
Instead of a presenting a long wishlist of desirable environmental actions, the Commission review should concentrate on setting a few priorities and actually getting them carried out, she said.

The Commission had promised Austria, Finland and Sweden it would find a way of bringing EU environmental protection standards up to the level set in the three new member states but it had not done so, Dybkjaer said.

Other areas where the environment committee thought concrete action was vital include reforming the Common Agriculture Policy before further EU enlargement and reducing the pollution caused by the transport, energy and tourist sectors.

Dybkjaer acknowledged the member states were worried about respecting the stringent economic criteria for joining a single EU currency, while encouraging industrial competitiveness and jobs, and did not always feel they had the cash to spend on protecting the environment.
In that case, they and the Commission should not pay lip service to environmental ideals and come clean.
"They should tell the truth. They should say we can't afford to do more, we have other priorities. They should concentrate on what they can do and then do it," she said.
In any case, the Danish Liberal feels more can be done with existing means if there is the will.
"Denmark has shown you can control energy consumption if you want. We have had 50 percent growth in gross national product since 1972 but zero growth in energy consumption.

"Denmark has high energy prices but it is one of the few countries which can actually respect the convergence criteria. And because we have high energy taxation, we don't need to tax other things, like labour or goods."
Dybkjaer said she expected EU Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard would next week say the Commission could not accept most of Parliament's amendments.

But she said she was not in conflict with the Danish commissioner, who was obliged to speak on behalf of the whole Commission and needed the Parliament to be firm on environmental issues to push decent legislation through.
The review of the 5th action plan needs the approval of both MEPs and ministers to come into force.
Dybkjaer predicted reaching agreement with the Council of Ministers would be difficult.
"Everyone thinks conciliation talks will be necessary," she said.
